description: The affordance that injects an "App settings" control into the Control UI's sidebar footer, and the host bridge it calls to open the app's own settings surface. This file is the ONE owner of that injected script: core/app-settings-affordance.js reads it (the desktop reads that module and installs the script into the gateway page over executeJavaScript; the iOS client bundles THIS FILE and installs it through a WKUserScript), so there is one copy of the injected script in the tree rather than one per client. The desktop and the phone run identical bytes; only the host bridge differs, and only in how it is wired.
why: The Control UI is upstream and its DOM is free to change at any release, so the affordance is DEFENSIVE by construction. It locates the footer by a stable selector, falls back to the footer bar and then to a fixed corner if the exact node is gone, and every step is wrapped so a change to the host page cannot throw into it. A Control UI update must be able to move the footer without breaking the page or stranding app settings.

The affordance never reimplements settings: it only opens the shared surface, by calling a host bridge the client installs. That bridge is the ONE thing that differs between clients: the desktop points `__clawAppSettings.open` at an IPC that runs openSettings(), and the phone points it at a WKScriptMessageHandler that raises its sheet.

The bridge global and the CONFIG global are two different names on purpose. The desktop installs its bridge through Electron's contextBridge, which exposes a FROZEN, non-writable property: the script must never assign to it or merge onto it, or a strict-mode reassignment throws in the page (measured 2026-09-16, `Script failed to execute`). So the label, tooltip, tokens and anchors arrive on their own plain global `__clawAppSettingsConfig`, which the client sets with an ordinary assignment, and the script only ever READS the bridge.

It is an ARRAY of lines rather than one escaped string, the same shape as prompt-metadata's hook, because a maintainable escape is the only kind that survives an edit: each line here is a line of the script, a diff reads as a diff, and the readers join it with a newline.

The tokens are handed in resolved rather than read from the page, because the affordance is styled to read as part of the footer and the token layer is core/spec/tokens.json's to own. The script falls back to the page's own currentColor and neutral values when a token is absent, so it reads as part of the footer before any theme has been resolved.
script: try { if (window.console && console.debug) console.debug('[claw] app-settings affordance: ' + message); } catch (e) {}
// The config is a plain global the client sets with an ordinary assignment.
// The bridge is separate and may be a frozen contextBridge object, so it is
if (bridge && typeof bridge.open === 'function') { bridge.open(); return true; }
log('no host bridge to open app settings');
// The one route that never depends on the injected node existing: open() is
// reachable whether or not a button was ever placed, so a page whose footer
// we could not find still has app settings one call away. Set on the config
// global (which is writable) rather than on the frozen bridge. The client
// also has a native fallback of its own (a menu item on the desktop, the
// corner button on iOS); this is the page-side half of that promise.
try { window.__clawAppSettingsConfig = config; config.openAppSettings = open; } catch (e) {}
// A gear glyph as inline SVG, so the control carries no dependency on the
// host page's own icon set, which is free to change.
// Place the control, defensively. The primary anchor is the footer's own
// row of action buttons, where it sits beside the gateway settings control;
// the footer bar is the fallback if that row is gone, and a fixed corner is
// the last resort so the affordance is reachable even when the whole footer
// has been restructured. FAIL SOFT: a placement that finds nothing returns
// false rather than throwing, and the client's native route still opens
if (actions) { actions.appendChild(button); log('placed in footer actions'); return true; }
if (footer) { footer.appendChild(button); log('placed in footer bar (fallback)'); return true; }
} catch (e) { log('place threw: ' + e); return false; }
} catch (e) { log('ensure threw: ' + e); return false; }
// The footer renders after boot and re-renders on navigation, and a
// re-render can drop our node, so watch for it and put it back. The
// observer is the whole reason a one-shot placement is not enough: the
// Control UI is a single-page app that rebuilds its sidebar.
